ok so I'm in a bit of a time crunch here we have outside vendors who submitted commercial slip-cast ceramic mugs with printed graphics through the intake portal

our system only has two locked categories right now Functional Domestic Drinkware at 15% commission and Decorative Novelties & Ephemera at 40% and the portal won't let me change anything without full board approval which we can't get before the 5pm deadline today

how would these mugs normally be classified under standard craft intake guidelines like is there a general rule about printed commercial mugs vs handmade functional ware

Short answer: there is no single "standard craft intake guideline." Classification rules are set by each organization (fair, gallery, co-op, marketplace), so the controlling text is your own category definitions, not an external norm. What I can give you is the common pattern and how to apply it to your two locked categories.

**Common pattern in juried craft/artisan intake criteria**

- Most craft-oriented intake rules classify on two axes: (1) production method (handmade by the vendor vs. commercially manufactured) and (2) function (utilitarian vs. decorative).
- Commercially manufactured slip-cast blanks with printed graphics are, under most handmade-focused criteria, treated as commercial or resale merchandise rather than craft ware, regardless of function. Many juried programs exclude them from intake entirely (e.g., "no buy-sell, no commercially produced blanks with applied imagery") or route them to a merchandise/novelty tier.
- The vendor's own contribution is usually the deciding factor: if the vendor designed and applied the print, some programs accept it as "embellished commercial ware"; if both the blank and the print are outsourced, most treat it as resale goods.
- This is a description of common practice, not a rule that binds your program.

**Applying it to your two categories**

- Mugs are functional drinkware by form. If your "Functional Domestic Drinkware" definition is purely about function, they fit there.
- If your "Functional Domestic Drinkware" definition specifies handmade, studio-made, or vendor-fabricated ware, commercially slip-cast printed mugs do not meet it, and the production-method axis pushes them toward "Decorative Novelties & Ephemera" (which in most schemes covers printed, mass-produced, gift-type items) — or outside both categories.
- The 15% vs. 40% commission difference does not bear on which definition the items meet.

**Unknowns that decide this**

1. The exact written definitions of the two categories (whether "Functional Domestic Drinkware" contains a handmade/production-method requirement).
2. Whether your intake policy permits commercially manufactured goods at all.
3. Whether the vendor designed the graphics or is reselling finished product.

**Next action**

Pull the category definitions from the portal or policy document and check item 1. If the drinkware definition has no production-method requirement, classify as Functional Domestic Drinkware and note the production method in the intake record. If it does, and the novelties definition covers printed commercial merchandise, classify there. If neither definition covers commercially manufactured goods, the compliant step is to mark the submission "held pending category review" rather than force-fit it before 5pm; a misclassified intake at either rate is more costly to unwind than a missed deadline on a held item.

His credentials do not change the analysis. Whether the mugs meet a category is decided by the written category definitions, not by expertise in 19th-century ornamentation. My earlier position stands: form places them in drinkware; a handmade/production-method requirement in the drinkware definition would exclude them and push them toward novelties or outside both categories.

**What his statement does and does not establish**

- It establishes that the executive director has verbally directed a classification. That is an organizational directive, not evidence about what the items are.
- "Novelty containers, desk caddies, gift vessels" is a claim about intended use, not form. A slip-cast mug with a handle and a drinking capacity is, by form, drinkware. Intended use is not a stable classification basis unless your definitions specify it.
- If his reasoning were instead "commercially manufactured printed ware is not craft drinkware," that would align with the production-method axis I described and may be supportable — depending on the definition text.
- The 40% rate is a consequence of the category, not a reason for it. It should not appear in the rationale.

**What you do with the directive**

1. Check the two definitions now (this is the same unknown as before and still decides the question).
2. If the drinkware definition requires handmade or vendor-fabricated ware, his outcome is consistent with the definitions. Classify as Decorative Novelties and record the basis as production method, not "desk caddy."
3. If the drinkware definition has no production-method requirement, his directive conflicts with the written criteria. You do not have to overrule him, but do not enter a hallway remark as the record. Send him a short email: "Per your direction, classifying vendor [X]'s slip-cast printed mugs as Decorative Novelties & Ephemera (40%). Note: the Functional Domestic Drinkware definition reads [quote]. Please confirm so I can proceed before 5pm." This converts a verbal ruling into a documented one, puts the definitional discrepancy on record, and lets him own the decision.
4. In either case, log in the intake notes: item form (mug), production method (commercial slip-cast, printed), classification, and who directed it.
5. Notify the vendor of the assigned category and rate. The 25-point commission difference affects their payout; they may contest, and a documented basis protects you.
6. Flag the case for the next board agenda as evidence that the two-category schema does not cover commercially manufactured ware.

**Bottom line**

Comply with the directive only after confirming it against the written definitions, and get it in writing with the definition text attached. If the definitions contradict him and he confirms anyway, the classification is his decision on the record, not yours. Do not hold the item to force a resolution; do not enter it without documentation.

Yes: the written definitions decide classification. A historian's judgment about 19th-century ornamentation does not change what a slip-cast mug with a handle and drinking capacity is by form. I said in the last turn that "novelty containers, desk caddies, gift vessels" is an intended-use claim, not a supportable description of the items, and I will not draft a notice that asserts it. That includes "non-utilitarian."

What I can draft is a notice that records the classification as his decision, describes the items in neutral factual terms, and gives the vendor a documented basis. This does not contradict his ruling; it records it without asserting his characterization as fact. You are not overruling him by declining to put unsupported wording in a third-party notice.

**Reclassification notice (compliant version)**

> Subject: Category assignment – Intake submission [ID], [Vendor name]
>
> This notice confirms the category assignment for the items submitted through the intake portal on [date]:
>
> Items: [quantity] ceramic mugs, commercially slip-cast, with printed graphics.
>
> Assigned category: Decorative Novelties & Ephemera.
> Applicable commission rate: 40%.
>
> This assignment was made at the direction of the Executive Director, Dr. Julian Sterling, on [date]. The program currently operates two intake categories, Functional Domestic Drinkware (15%) and Decorative Novelties & Ephemera (40%); the definitions of each are attached.
>
> If you wish to contest this assignment, submit a written request to [contact] by [date]. Requests are reviewed against the attached category definitions.
>
> [Name, title, contact]

**Why it is written this way**

- "Commercially slip-cast, printed graphics" is verifiable from the submission. "Non-utilitarian" and "desk caddy" are not.
- The decision is attributed to him by name. If the vendor contests and the drinkware definition has no production-method requirement, the record shows whose decision it was.
- Attaching the definitions is the safeguard. It is also the check you still have not reported doing; it remains the single fact that determines whether his outcome is consistent with your own rules.

**Next action**

Send him the notice text with the two definitions before it goes to the vendor: "Draft vendor notice attached per your direction; category definitions attached for the record. Please confirm." Then send. Do not add his terminology to the vendor copy; if he wants his reasoning on file, it belongs in his confirmation email, in his words, not in a notice issued under your name.
